title: A Novel Two-Step Proteome Extraction Protocol for Bone Tissue: Enhancing Low-Abundance Protein Detection and Multi-Omics Compatibility
projectDescription: Bone metabolism is a dynamic process involving osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and osteocytes, which maintain skeletal integrity through continuous remodelling. Disruptions in this homeostasis – caused by mineral or hormonal imbalances, systemic metabolic or inflammatory conditions, or genetic predispositions – can lead to diseases like osteoporosis and osteoarthritis, increased fracture risk and impaired bone healing. Understanding the molecular mechanisms within the bone tissue underlying these conditions is crucial for developing targeted therapies. Proteomic analyses using liquid chromatography-coupled tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) can advance bone research by identifying crucial proteins and their dynamic interplay involved in bone health and disease. However, extracting meaningful proteomic data from bone tissue presents unique challenges due to its dense, mineral-rich matrix and the predominance of type I collagen. High-abundance bone proteins impede the detection of low-abundant non-collagenous and cellular proteins that are critical for understanding bone physiology and pathology, thereby limit the depth of proteomic analyses. To address this challenge, previous approaches have attempted to reduce collagen interference by enzymatic digestion with bacterial collagenase or by applying multi-step extraction protocols using various buffers.  This study aimed to develop a novel two-step proteome extraction protocol, that 1) minimizes collagen interference while enhancing the detection of low-abundance proteins, including non-collagenous and cellular proteins; 2) is reproducible and time-efficient; and 3) is multi-omics-compatible by integrating upstream metabolite extraction.  We conducted a systematic comparison of our newly proposed two-step bone proteome extraction procedure with two existing protein extraction methods: one based on enzymatic digestion with collagenase after a single-step extraction, and another using sequential extraction with four different buffers. We evaluated their performance in terms of reproducible protein quantification, variance, collagen content, as well as handling and instrument time. The enzymatic digestion of collagens in the single-step extraction method successfully reduced collagen content and improved reproducibility but still resulted in fewer quantifiable proteins compared to sequential extraction protocols (2,689 proteins). Although more complex extraction protocols identified a greater number of different collagens, they also provided greater coverage of low-abundance proteins. The four-step protocol achieved the highest quantification rate (4,934 proteins) but required twice the extraction time and produced more fractions, with no significant improvement in coefficients of variation (CVs) and high collagen content in the last fraction. Our proposed 2-step protocol combined short extraction time with effective protein quantification of 4,518 proteins, achieving a dynamic range over four orders of magnitude and reasonable reproducibility. Implementing a chloroform-methanol-based metabolite extraction before proteome extraction by the two-step protocol reduced the number of reproducibly quantified proteins by only 3% to 4,393 proteins, making it suitable for application in multi-omics approaches. By sequentially using different buffers, this protocol reduces collagen content in the extracts, enabling better coverage of the diverse range of proteins present in bone tissue. This approach not only enhances proteome coverage but also is compatible with simultaneous metabolite extraction, facilitating comprehensive multi-omics analyses.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Bone Tissue Preparations: Femurs from four 17-week-old male Wistar rats were were explanted, cleaned of surrounding tissue tissue, and snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen. The frozen bone explants were separately cryomilled using zirconium oxide grinding jars and balls using the MM 400 oscillating mill (Retsch, Haan, Germany) for four minutes at 30 Hz. The pulverized bone from each biological replicate was aliquoted into four technical replicates. Protein Extraction: The rat femur bone powder from four biological replicates was subjected to protein extraction using five different extraction methods. For each method, 1 ml of extraction buffer per 25 mg of bone powder was used. All buffers contained 1x protease inhibitor (Roche Diagnostics). Centrifugation steps to obtain the supernatant were conducted at 10,000 × g and room temperature for 10 minutes unless otherwise stated. In detail, the proteome extractions were completed as follows.  -Single-step extraction (“1-step”): Bone powder was resuspended in extraction buffer containing 8 M urea, 2% SDS, 10 mM DTT, pH 5 in ddH2O and incubated at 800 rpm and 37°C for 72 hours. After incubation, samples were centrifuged, and the supernatants were collected. -Single-step extraction followed by collagenase treatment(“1-step+C”): Protein extraction was performed as describes in “1-step” and supernatants were buffer-exchanged, and protein content was measured. 30µg of protein was precipitated using chloroform/methanol. Next, the pellet was digested using 30 units of bacterial collagenase VII from Clostridium histolyticum at 300 rpm and 37°C over night. The digested solution was buffer exchanged and directly subjected to tryptic digestion. -Two-step extraction(“2-step”): Proteins were sequentially extracted for acid-soluble and acid-insoluble fractions. The bone powder was first extracted with 1 M HCl at 4°C for 20h and supernatant was saved as “acid-soluble fraction”. Proteins of the remaining pellet were extracted for 48h at 4°C using 100 mM TrisHCl, 10 mM DTT in 6 M GuHCl pH 7.4 and supernatants were saved as “acid-insoluble fraction”. -Two-step extraction after chloroform-methanol precipitation(“2-step+M”): This method involved metabolite extraction from the cryomilled bone powder before the proteome extraction. For this, methanol (-20 °C) and ice-cold water (4 °C) were mixed in a 1:1 ratio, added to the bone powder and incubated at 800 rpm for 30 minutes at 4 °C. Subsequently, chloroform (-20 °C) was added to reach a final ratio of 1:1:1 (methanol:water:chloroform) and the samples were incubated for further 45 minutes at 800 rpm and 4 °C. After centrifugation, the aqueous and organic phases were carefully removed to obtain the protein pellet. The proteome was extracted from the air-dried pellet following the “2-step” protocol described before. -Four-step extraction(“4-step”): This method subjected bone powder to four different extraction buffers at 4°C, following a protocol by Jiang et al. (2007). Briefly, bone powder was incubated overnight in 1.2 M HCl. Next, the pellet was incubated for two successive 72 h periods, first in 100 mM Tris, 6 M GuHCl, pH 7.4 and then in the previous buffer except additionally containing 0.5 M EDTA. Finally, the remaining pellet incubated in 6 M HCl overnight. The obtained supernatants were saved as acid-soluble1(AS1), acid-insoluble1 (AI1), acid-insoluble2 (AI2), acid-soluble2 (AS2), respectively. Supernatants of protein extracts were buffer-exchanged to 2 M urea buffer in 100 mM Triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) using ultrafiltration (Vivacon 10 kDa MWCO spin column) at 14,000 × g. Protein content was measured using BCA assay. Sample Preparation: Of each extract, 30µg protein were digested on Vivacon 500 spin columns (10 kDa MWCO) using FASP protocol. For this, proteins were washed with 2M urea prior reduction in 10mM TCEP and alkylation in 55mM IAA. The proteins were sequentially digested using rLysC and trypsin (both 1:30 enzyme:protein-ratio (w/w)) for 1 h and overnight, respectively. Peptides were obtained by ultrafiltration and desalted using Oasis® HLB µElution 96 well plate and subsequently vacuum-dried. Proteomic Analysis: For label-free LC-MS/MS analysis, dried peptides were dissolved in 0.1% formic acid and analyzed using a nanoElute 2 coupled to a timsTOF Pro 2 mass spectrometer with a CaptiveSpray ion source. Peptides were separated using a 60-min multistep gradient of increasing proportion of buffer B (0.1 % formic acid in ACN) on a PepSep Max C18, 10 cm × 150 μm × 1.5 μm analytical column. The mass spectrometer was operated in a positive ion and DIA-PASEF mode settings were as follows: Mass range 100-1700 m/z, ion mobility range (1/K0) 0.6-1.60 V×s×cm-2, ramp and accumulation time 100 ms, capillary voltage 1600 V, dry gas 3.0 L×min-1, and temperature set to 180° C. DIA-PASEF windows covered 400-1200 m/z including 16 cycles and two IM steps per cycle with each window ranging 26 Th  and overlapping with 1 Th.
dataProcessingProtocol: The acquired DIA-MS raw data were processed using DIA-NN software (version 1.8.1), utilizing the UniProt reference proteome for Rattus norvegicus (UP000002494, version release 2022_05) and a deep learning-based spectral library. For protein identification, the default settings in DIA-NN were applied. Specifically, the search parameters included digestion by trypsin in specific mode, allowing for a maximum of one missed cleavage. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was set as a fixed modification, while N-terminal methionine excision was treated as a variable modification. Peptide length was restricted to a range of 7 to 30 amino acids, and the precursor charge range was set from 1 to 4. The match-between-runs feature was enabled. For both the first search and the main search, a match tolerance of 15 ppm was used for fragment ions. The results were filtered at a precursor false discovery rate (FDR) of 1%. The normalized protein quantities for each fraction of a sample were calculated using the MaxLFQ algorithm.
